transcript.title: MICHAEL WATSON, MISSISSIPPI SECRETARY OF STATE, Petitioner, v. REPUBLICAN NATIONAL COMMITTEE, ET AL., Respondents

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: We will hear argument this morning in Case 24-1260, Watson versus Republican National Committee.  Mr. Stewart.

Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court:  States have broad power over elections.  Throughout our history, they've used that power to change how they hold elections.  Nowhere is that change more apparent than in Election Day itself.  Congress set the federal Election Day in 1845.  At the time, everyone voted in person.  There was no  absentee voting.  There was no secret ballot. Voters challenged each other's qualifications at the polls on Election Day, and states received ballots on Election Day.  Over time, states changed all those practices.  They did so as Congress extended Election Day to all federal offices.  They've done so ever since.  No one claims that in setting the federal Election Day Congress blocked most of those changes.  The dispute is whether Congress  blocked just one change, allowing ballots cast by Election Day to be received after that day. States have allowed that for over a century. Congress has respected it.  No one challenged it until now.  The question is whether Congress in 1845 blocked that practice.  The answer is no.  The Election Day statutes adopt a simple rule:  States must make a final choice of officers by Election Day.  That is the plain meaning of an election.  As this Court said in United States versus  Classic, from time immemorial, an election to public office has been, in point of substance, no more and no less than the expression by qualified electors of their choice of candidates.  Mississippi satisfies that rule.  It makes a choice on Election Day.  And only that  rule respects the last 180 years of state lawmaking.  If Election Day must be what it was in 1845, that takes out much more than the ballot receipt laws of 30 states today.  It dooms absentee voting, modern methods of voting, the secret ballot, and more.  Congress did not adopt that destabilizing view when it simply set the Election Day.  The Fifth Circuit was wrong to rule otherwise.  This Court should reverse.  I welcome the Court's questions.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Just to be clear, you have  --you said in your opening statement sometimes, you said, the decision -- the choice  has to be made by Election Day, and at other points, you say on Election Day.  Which is it?

I -- I think the statewide choice needs to make -- be made by Elect -- or -- or on Election Day itself, when the entire electorate has voted, Justice Thomas.  I think voters themselves need -- need  to make their individual selections by Election Day.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: If I give my ballot, mail-in ballot, to my neighbor, is that a choice?
It's a choice.  It's not a final choice that can be recognized in the context of an election.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: So when do I know whether or not a choice is final?
When you've submitted to the state, to the appropriate state election , through the designated state process.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: So why isn't it the rule then that the final  --or the formalized decision, electoral decision, isn't made until that's done?
Until -- until it's submitted to the official, Your Honor.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Yeah.
I think  -- I mean, I think the choice is made once the voter has made  --the voters as -- as a whole have made an irrevocable decision by casting ballots.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: What does that mean?
A final  -- a final choice.  They've -- they've cast their ballots.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, if  -- I made a final choice when I handed it to my neighbor.
But it's a final choice within an official state process, Justice Thomas, which  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, I think the ballot is an official state process.  Is that enough?
Not enough to be known in a public way to the state.  That happens when it is parted with and submitted through -- through mail to the  --to the appropriate election official.  Then it's final.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: If  -- if "day" means -- includes a period after a particular day of the election, does -- does it include a  particular day before the day of the election?  Or does your logic require a different consideration?

Forgive me if I -- I may not be understanding the question correctly, Your Honor, but I think the key is that the Election Day is the day by which a final choice electorate-wide must be made.  It can't be made after that day by voters or  -- or the electorate as a whole.  But individual selections can surely be made before that day  because there's still no final choice until you have a -- an electorate-wide deadline.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Is there any limit to that?
As to how early people could vote?

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Sure.  Yeah, they fill out a ballot if you're giving them a ballot and, you know, drop it off two weeks before.

As far as the federal Election Day statutes are concerned, Your Honor, I don't think there -- there is a limit  to how early that could occur.  I think you just need the day when the electorate as a whole needs to have chosen.  There might be other practical or other barriers in that.  Of course, elect  -- elections are a very long process to begin with, the entire electoral process, so, surely, things are happening weeks and months before. But I think even a couple weeks before, even earlier than that in some cases, people are making individual selections.  It's just  Election Day itself is the day for the final collective choice.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Counsel, I under -- I want to go back to your answers to Justice Thomas.  So I understand that Mississippi's particular rule says that it has to be deposited in USPS or with a common carrier, but I don't understand why Mississippi's definition in the next case would preclude a state from adopting a law along the lines of the one that Justice Thomas is proposing.  For example, if I have someone in my neighborhood in my HOA who says, listen, I'm going to take everybody's votes in, what if the state said that's fine; if you've cast your  final vote and you've -- you know, you've designated someone to carry your vote to  -- as long as it gets to the ballot box five days after Election Day, it's fine.  Why does your definition preclude what Justice Thomas hypothesized?

Right.  And I think, Justice Barrett, the answer is that submission to mail or common carrier is  --is different in kind than, say, submitting it to a relative or  -- or sort of a neighbor in that way.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: What's the difference?  They're not government officials.
They  --they are impartial third parties that have a duty to deliver what they're owed without altering it.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: But what about the definition that you're proposing precludes that?  Your definition didn't say final as  submitted to an impartial third party or final as submitted to a common carrier.  You said the final choice has been made.  And there are lots of different ways, it seems to me, that you could make a final choice.  And you also have the problem of this  revocability from the Postal Service regulation.

So -- so I think, to start with the first part, Your Honor, I mean, I  -- I think we're going at a historically recognized form of finality.  I think history is  -- is helpful in a number of ways, and one way is that as long as we've had mail-in voting, we -- we have -- for almost as long as that time, we  --we've had post-Election Day ballot receipt.  I mean, mail-in voting I think in general has been understood as a permissible, unchallenged method of  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: I wouldn't rely on the history if I were you since you're telling  us not to rely on the other side's history, like just because it's always been done that way doesn't mean it has to be done that way, which I actually find as a good point in your favor, but then it seems to me that you're flipping back around and saying, well, absentee  voting has always been done that way by common carrier, and so that's how we would expect it to be done.

Well, I think it says something that for a hundred years we've -- we've had people voting by mail and that's been an understood means of submitting a ballot to the state.  I think what it embodies, Justice Barrett, is there's an intuition that when you send  --when you put something through the Postal Service, it's final, it's trusted, it's  --it's not like giving it to kind of a non-official  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well  --
-- third party.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, what  --what if  -- what if a state came up with a law that said so long as a notary, that's official,  that's recognized, certified that you cast your ballot on Election Day and it was delivered later by whatever means, common carrier or not, what  --what in your theory of the preemptive effect of this statute would preclude that law?
I think two points on that, Justice Gorsuch.  One I think is that --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Pick your best. (Laughter.)
Well, I think one's kind of in -- a point in our favor and one -- one's kind of a point against our friends, which is that there's a finality of submitting it to an and  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Yeah, it's been -- it's been notarized by -- well, how about a justice of the United States Supreme Court.  Is  that official enough for you?
I mean, it -- it -- it's pretty official.  I don't think it's been submitted  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: It's pretty .  (Laughter.)
It's  --it's pretty good, Your Honor, but I don't -- I don't think it kind of hits submission to the state.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Ah.  Okay.  Well, that  --I wanted to explore -- so -- so that's not submitted to the state?  Even if it's notarized, an  --an affidavit, it was final on the day of and somebody brings it in to the state offices a week or three months later,  that doesn't count, but if it goes into the mail, it does?  What in the statute  --what words in the statute would you have us read that into, that rule into?
Well, I mean, I -- I think -- I mean, just to make sure I understand, I  --I think that's fine under my friend's view too, Your Honor.  I mean, a notary could be  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: I'm asking about your view, counsel.
Sure.  So I  --I think --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: You're saying that's not fine, and I want to understand what -- what  --what in the federal law preempts that.
Well, I think, number one, I -- I just am not -- at least as I'm understanding the hypothetical, it doesn't appear to be submission to the state, Your Honor, in the same --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Oh, it gets submitted to the state three weeks later, just not by common carrier.
Well, I mean, if -- I mean, if what you're saying, Your Honor, is it's  --that a  --that a notary has been deemed a sufficient ballot receiver under state law, then I think  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Yes.  Then that's okay too?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Okay.  What if state law  -- so now you're saying that is okay.
I -- I think it -- it may  -- you know, it may depend on how -- you know, what the level of officiality is at the time.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, the  -- the state says it's official, by God, when -- when a Supreme Court justice or -- or perhaps just a  notary says it's official, that's good enough under your theory.  It has to be, I think.  And if that's okay, why can't a state say:  How about a time -stamped video showing that I voted on Election Day?  Here I am filling out my ballot, and then -- and --and then my brother or maybe some aggregator of ballots brings it in a week or three later.
And  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: That's got to be okay too, doesn't it?
I -- I think it's still just  --I -- I -- I keep coming back, Justice Gorsuch, to this pedigree of submitting it to a state.  I mean, I think, as a good example --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, the state says that's official, the state says that's fine, ballot aggregators are great, and so long as it's a time -stamped video or a notary or maybe a Supreme Court, or who knows what, the librarian says you cast it on -- on the day of the election, we're good -- we're good to go, right?
I mean, I -- I do -- I do  -- do still have some concern that it has not been submitted through --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Counsel, why are you fighting the premise?  In the Civil War, at least two states permitted military officers who weren't sworn state officials, they were federal officials but not sworn state s, to accept the ballots and transmit  it by mail to the state, okay?  And that was in the Civil War, all right?  Since 1918, we've had laws like Mississippi.  By 1944, eight of them.  By -- since then, 12 more by 1886.  And now half the states permit absentee ballots that are dropped in the mail, correct?  No different than in the Civil War.  We have no federal law that says that's not okay for the state to designate someone by whom an official ballot has to be given by Election Day, correct?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: And if the state wants to make it a notary republic, if it wants to make it a military officer, if it wants to make it a Supreme Court justice, if it wants to make it anyone, as long as it's done by Election Day, that's what counts, correct?
I mean, I think that's possible.  We're not quite asking for that, Your Honor.  I really don't mean to fight the premise.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: No, you don't because you're only defending this law.  And  this law is very consistent with what happened in the Civil War.  It's very consistent with  what has happened for over a hundred years.  There's nothing in federal law that has prohibited it explicitly, correct?
That  --that's right, Your Honor.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: All right.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, Justice Sotomayor is asking you what I think she intends to be a friendly question, but maybe  you want to think about whether you want to go that far.  What if the state designates in  -- an of the Republican Party or the Democratic Party who receives these ballots,  collects ballots, and fills out an affidavit saying, I received all these and -- and I -- I will faithfully deliver them?  Would that be okay?

Well, I think it's  --I think it's actually okay under my friend's view, Your Honor.  We're not -- we're not making that ask.  I mean, as far as my friend's view are concerned, so long as somebody's designated a ballot receiver, they can be fine.  Party boss, party bag man, relative, any of those, so long  as the state says you are a ballot receiver, that's fine.  The only thing that apparently is not fine is a U.S. Postal Service common carrier.  And I think that is, I think, very -- a very odd way to read those statutes --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, the Postal Service is not part of the state, and a common carrier isn't part of any government.

It's  --that's right, Your Honor.  But, I mean, certainly, we all  know the status of the U.S. Postal Service is a highly regulated government entity with certain obligations.  Common carriers in a very similar way, high  --highly regulated with similar obligations. And they give -- in both cases, they're imbued with a duty to deliver what they receive.  And, in fact, a duty that's, I  --I think, a good example -- maybe a good example is the fact that the IRS accepts tax returns, which are obviously highly consequential documents with key timeliness requirements, the  IRS accepts tax returns both through the mail and through common carriers.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, you will -- you will accept ballots that are received within five days after Election Day, that what -- what  is, you know, the whatever -- the -- the date that's -- that's set as Election Day, right?
That's right, Your Honor.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: And you have a variety of line-drawing problems.  So we've been exploring one, to whom and by what means is this thing to be -- the ballot to be delivered to the state.  But how -- what -- what about the length of time that a state could choose?  Is it the case  -- isn't it the case that some state allows -- will -- will count ballots that are received 21 days after Election Day?
There are a couple that at the outlier it's kind of canvassing and it  can go that far.  I think more common is about --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, is that okay? Is that all right?

As far as -- as far as the federal Election Day statutes are concerned, yes, Your Honor.  And I think this  actually gets to a good point that -- that loops back to something Justice Gorsuch was mentioning, was  -- was getting at in a certain way, which I think he was saying, one, the  federal Election Day statutes decides that.  I -- I think that's the key point in our favor, is this  --this is an area where states get to go first to make these decisions. Congress can step in, but the idea  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: So there's no limit? Except I suppose the day when the presidential electors have to be appointed or the day when the  --the next Congress begins, starts its session, that's the only limit on counting -- on counting mail -in ballots?

Those are some of the limits, Your Honor.  But I'd also say the  federal Election Day statutes don't require states to count ballots at all.  It doesn't speak to counting, period.  So, I mean, if a state really didn't want to  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Not  -- not counting but  --but being delivered.  So I do think it is a consequence, and you can tell me if I'm wrong, but just so we can wrap this up, that by  any means and by any date up until the next Congress meets, a state can receive ballots?

I think, for congressional races, potentially, yes, Your Honor.  I think there -- there are other Title  III kind of things that push action earlier in the presidential context, but, again, I mean, there's nothing  -- the key question is these are one  -- three one-sentence provisions,  and we want to be, I think, very careful not to read them for more than they're worth.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: And, counsel, isn't --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Counsel  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: I was just going to say, isn't -- isn't your point that the line-drawing issues that have been raised are only problems to the extent that Congress thought they were problems?  We're  -- we're in a preemption dynamic, and so the question I think really is, what did Congress intend with its statement about Election Day?  Did it mean  to cabin the states so that they did not have the discretion to make these kinds of decisions?  And, in addition to what Justice Sotomayor has said, which is we have no federal statute that precludes this, I think we have several stat  -- federal statutes that suggest that Congress was aware of post-Election Day ballot deadlines that the states had enacted  and, in fact, incorporated those in several circumstances.  So can you speak to that?  I'm  -- I'm talking about UOCAVA, for example, and some  other federal statutes that indicate that Congress not only knew this was going on, but then it interpreted and incorporated the state's own post -ballot -- post-Election Day ballot deadlines into federal law.

Sure, Your Honor.  So I  -- I -- I think that's exactly right.  So UOCAVA is  --is maybe the best example where Congress was told that about a dozen or so states have post -Election Day ballot receipt laws.  It respected those explicitly as to a deadline for  -- for ballots in  -- in --in that law.  I think the United States has agreed with us on -- on that very point.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: And Congress wasn't worried, I think, about the states picking dates that were, you know, we might think are too long or whatnot.  That  --that was not in the statute.  Congress just said whatever the state has decided with regard to ballot receipt  deadlines is going to apply here, correct?

Right.  And that's been the case for 180 years, Your Honor.  And I think one feature that I  --you know, obviously, we're -- we're -- we're searching for what did the statutes mean at the time, but I think it's very hard for my -- my friends to explain a hundred  -- the past hundred years of history and this lawmaking.  The Soldier Voting Act in the 1940s was  --was another example where Congress recognized and respected state deadlines.  And it just  -- it gets very hard to explain those things if you don't adopt the view that the federal Election Day statutes just do not set a ballot receipt deadline.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: I want to ask you about the recall problem, and before I get to that, throughout your brief, you say that the  -- that the federal statute does require voters to submit their ballots to election s on Election Day, must be cast by Election Day, and that the -- and that the Election Day is the day to conclude and consummate the election through a final selection.  You agree with all those statements in your brief?
Yes.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Okay.  But, at the same time, you say:  Actually, it doesn't have to be submitted to an election official; it  just has to be submitted to a common carrier. And there's a contradiction there that I -- I just want you to first address, and then I'll give you my hypothetical.
Very good, Your Honor. I think, when you put something in the mail, you're not -- I think --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: That's not an election official.  FedEx isn't an election .
Right, but the recipient certainly is the person who you're submitting -- submitting it in the mail to.  I mean, that is  --that is the recipient.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Sure.  Of course.
And, right, Your Honor. And I think --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: You submit it to FedEx and they deliver it to the election , but  --but you say it has to be submitted to an election official throughout your brief, but then you say a common carrier is okay, and that -- those two things don't add up.
Well, I think the difference is, say, you know, sending it to  your brother versus sending it to the registrar.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, we already dealt with that.  The brother turns out to be okay so long as the state says so.  You  --
I think that's okay on their view, Your Honor.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: It's also okay  --
I -- I'm a little more  --more guarded than that.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, you  -- I think you already answered that one.  So  -- so here's the hypo.  Let's say you have a state where a  large portion of the electorate mails in their ballots on or close to Election Day.  Not far-fetched.  Many states are like that.  Then the day after the election, a story breaks that one of the lead candidates engaged in an inappropriate sexual escapade or perhaps is concluding with a foreign power.  Again, not far-fetched, I think.  And the competing candidate immediately goes on the airwaves and urges voters to recall their ballots and  -- and  --and to tell the common carriers not to deliver them.  And many common carriers will do that with anything that you send through the -- through them.  FedEx, you just call them up and say I want it back.  In that hypothetical, did the election happen on Election Day?  Oh, by the way, it swings the election.  (Laughter.)

So the -- the election did happen on  --on Election Day, Justice Gorsuch.  As  --as we've explained, our ballot does not allow using mail recall, anything like  that.  When somebody submits their ballot by mail, it's final.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, just  --just first deal with my hypothetical, and then I'll deal with your statute.
Okay.  The -- the -- the election happened on Election Day.  It sounds like  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Even though it changes the outcome?
I mean, I think it  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Yes has to be your answer, doesn't it?
I mean -- I mean, yes, Your Honor.  I'm just --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Okay.
I -- I -- I want to be clear about the  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: All right.  And then  --
--we are not agreeing that the outcome can be properly changed in that circumstance.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, hold on.  It did in my circum --- in my hypothetical.  You can't change my hypothetical, counsel.  (Laughter.)
And I'm just saying it's unlawful, Your Honor.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: It's un  -- what's -- what's unlaw- --what --
I don't mean to disparage your hypothetical.  I'm just saying that it  --that it's an unlawful circumstance because we don't allow ballot -- ballot recall in our state.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Oh, in Mississippi, okay.  But -- but that hypothetical could  happen in another state, right?
I think, if the state is not providing that on mailing there's a final choice made, I think that would be a problem with that law under the federal statutes, Your Honor.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Okay.  Now you say your statute  -- you're -- you're -- you're different.  You admit my hypothetical could  happen, but you say it can't happen in Mississippi because recall's not allowed.  I couldn't find that anywhere in Mississippi law.  In fact, what I did see was a statute that says that you -- that the  Secretary of State can promulgate rules and regulations.  That's 23-15-637(3).  And then I went and looked at the regulations, and Rule 2.1 says that an absentee ballot is the final vote of a voter when the ballot is marked accepted.  That doesn't preclude recall.
And  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: In fact, that allows recall.
-- I --I don't -- I respectfully don't agree with that, Your Honor. I mean, what  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Where -- where does it say recall is not permitted?  I couldn't find that anywhere in your statutes or the rules.
And I think, by providing that ballots are final when cast under our statute itself  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: No, it doesn't.  It says they're final when marked accepted.
That's the regulation, Your Honor.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Yeah.  It's your  --
Yeah.  And it  -- and --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: It's your regulation, and it allows recall.
It does  -- respectfully, it does not allow recall, Your Honor.  The ballot is final when cast.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Show me where it -- would you read to me the provision that precludes it?
It's  --it's subsection (3) of the statute that my friends have challenged.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: I read you subsection (3) that says the Secretary of State can make rules.
And  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: And then I read you the rule.
To ensure that the ballots are final when cast.  They  -- the -- the key thing  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: But the rule says  --
-- is that ballots are final when cast.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: It says  --no. Votes promulgated by an absentee ballot with  the absentee ballot  -- person's absentee vote is final.  You can make rules about when  they're final, and what the rule says it is final when marked accepted.

And that's -- I mean, it's speaking to a processing rule about what to do when somebody's -- you know, when somebody's ballot potentially doesn't arrive on time.  They submit an affidavit ballot.  But I would come back to the -- the text of the  statute, Your Honor.  I mean, "final when cast" is  -- is what our law --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Mr. Stewart, I just want to ask a clarifying point to this.  Is it possible for a portion of Mississippi's statute to be unlawful, not  -- just --just go with me here  --a portion of Mississippi's statute to be unlawful insofar as it potentially permits recall, but still that, you know, would not address whether Mississippi's statute was  unlawful insofar as it allowed ballot receipt after Election Day?
Yes, Your Honor.  I mean, I think one possibility would be, like, hey, look, you need a more unambiguous finality  here and you need to foreclose recall, period, full stop.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Okay.  And  --and on this question, I just want to make sure I understand what you're saying.  When you said,  yes, my friends on the other side say it's okay for private parties to deliver just like you do, are you saying that's just a manner of receipt, and whether your -- whether the ballot is received before or after the election, on all sides, everybody agrees that absentee  ballots can be turned in by having, you know, the neighbor, the party operative, or whatever scoop them up and bring them to the -- the ballot box?

Your Honor, I mean, maybe -- you know, I'm not sure if I answered the earlier thing as crisply as I could.  I'm not comfortable with the neighbor piece.  I do have serious concerns about that.  I  -- I --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: But is that tied to the ballot receipt problem, or is that just tied to, hey, maybe this is an unlawful way of executing absentee balloting regardless of when the ballots make it to the official?
I think it's the finality of the choice that has to be done by Election Day.  And  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Okay.
-- my --my concern is that if you're not sending it by mail or common carrier  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: You're getting caught up, counsel, again.  Could you go back  to the question?  Justice Barrett is not arguing with you.
Fair, Your Honor.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: What she's saying and what you said earlier is -- and you believe that under your adversary's  -- the opposing counsel's theory, you can give it to the RNC operative, you can give it to anybody, and so  long as it's received on Election Day by the state, that's okay.  That's what you're saying your opposing counsel's saying.  And you're saying the only question before us is, if they  can designate an appropriate vehicle to transmit the votes, then that's okay.
I think I was saying the lat  --the latter part, yes, Your Honor.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Mm-hmm.

I actually think, under my friend's view, it's okay for -- like, a state can deem the ballot -- deem received when the party operative himself or herself receives it because all that person has to do is be a ballot receiver designated by the state.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Right.
And we're trying to hew more closely not just to the text but also the historical hundred-year-long you can submit it by mail.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Okay.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Thank you --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: So  --but the bottom line is that states can choose when the final vote has to be counted?
States have discretion over counting.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Exactly.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Thank you, counsel.  Justice Thomas, anything further?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Just as a point of clarification, without looking at the  subsequent history, what do you think the federal law required as far as the Election Day?

That the voters make a final choice by that day.  The  -- the way I'd boil it down, Justice Thomas, is choice is  critical and unchanging; method of making that choice is malleable.  And that does also explain all the subsequent history.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: And you don't have to formalize that choice?
You do by submit -- by parting with your ballot and submitting it to the state.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Have we had any  --

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Justice  -- Justice  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: I'm sorry.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: -- Alito?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Your position does require some difficult line-drawing problems, and maybe that's inevitable, but one is the degree of confidence that one must have in the  entity or person who transmits the ballot to the state.  We've talked about that.  One is  how long after the Election Day vote -- votes must be  -- votes can be received.  A third is whether it has to be postmarked.  Are there  -- aren't there quite a -- aren't there eight states that do not require a postmark for late ballots?

There are a number of states that don't require that, Your Honor.  I think postmarking is  --is good evidence that something has been timely submitted.  That's  kind of borne out in the tax context.  I -- I think, you know, if -- if somebody were challenging a law like that, it would potentially be a very different kind of a challenge.  They'd have to make sort of factual showings to challenge that ballots were not cast by Election Day but surely not this case.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, maybe these -- maybe it's inevitable that some sort of line-drawing decisions like these have to be made, unless the rule is anything goes, you know, states can do anything they want in this area.  We don't have a whole lot to go on here.  We have the phrase "Election Day" and we  have history.  If we looked just at the phrase "Election Day," what would we take from that?  I think you're  --you've been saying we're -- and we're moving in this direction.  We don't have Election Day anymore.  We have election month or we have election months.  I mean, the  --the early voting can start a month before the election.  The ballots can be  received a month after the election.

Well, I  -- I think the best way to read it, Your Honor, is that by setting Election Day, the Congress set the final choice day.  And that's the key thing, final choice day.  What Congress was concerned  about at the time was some states making final choices, say, a month before other states were making final choices and the distortions, the fraud, the risks that -- that that had. And when everybody's making a final choice on the same day, even if some individual choices are made before then, you're honoring the statutes, and I think -- you know, I think, Justice Alito, you made this observation, you know, not a lot to go on because the statutes  are just not very -- there's not a lot of prolixity there.  I think that's a point in favor of deference to the states.  You know, if Congress  has not spoken to something, especially in this context, where states are expressly empowered to regulate these things, that's a big point in favor of letting states continue to do so as they  --they have for a century.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Do you think it's legitimate for us to take into account Congress's desire  -- Congress's passage of the Election Day statutes for the purpose of  combatting fraud or the appearance of fraud and will and some of the briefs have argued that confidence in election outcomes can be seriously undermined if the apparent outcome of the election at  --on the day after the polls close is radically flipped by the acceptance later of a big stash of  --of ballots that flip the election or  -- yeah.
I think  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: You've got ballots that are delivered by somebody -- by -- you  know, by a neighbor and they're received a month after the election and they don't have postmarks.

I -- I think the best way to do it is to honor the statute's purpose by  --but doing so by respecting the statute's text and animating context.  And what these statutes were getting at was not just any kind of fraud writ large in all elections, which, you know, no statute could do, but a situation where, okay, you know, State 1 votes  -- you know, has their election on one day, ends it, and State 2  neighboring has its election three weeks later because the concern would be let's say State 1 goes for one party and then State 3 goes for the other party with a huge turnout for that other party. You could have potential fraud. People went across state lines and voted, or you could have the appearance of that sort of fraud even if it didn't actually happen, like  people just said, oh, my gosh, they voted for that person, I -- you know, big turnout. So I think that's the kind of thing that animated those statutes, whereas fraud writ large was not  --was not a good example. I do think it's  --it's notable that my  --my friends with the United States, you know  --you know, obviously, they  -- they -- they've sounded the antifraud theme.  They  haven't cited a single example of fraud from post-Election Day ballot receipt in this century.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: All right.  Okay. Thank you.  I'll let my colleagues have a chance.
Thank you.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Justice Sotomayor?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Has there been any history of voter recall in the mails in -- in Mississippi?  You say the law doesn't permit it, but has there been any history of it?
None that I've ever heard of, Your Honor.  I mean, this isn't something that was raised until the appellate reply briefs.  And nobody cited a single example in history of it.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: All right.  And I understand Justice Alito's questions about the  policy questions of what will create discomfort or not.  But the Constitution vests the issue  of elections in the states unless superseded by Congress, correct?
That's right, Your Honor.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: So, if there is a policy question to be had, the entities to decide that are the states and Congress, not the courts, correct?
That's right, Your Honor.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: And absent a law in federal law that suggests that absentee  ballots must be received by a certain time, there's no explicit requirement of that, correct?
Right, Your Honor, or even implicit.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: And -- and the implicit, we have the military acts that since World War II at least and the Civil War -- I should go back that far  -- have permitted absentee ballots to be received long past Election Day, correct?
We have a very long history of that, Your Honor.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Exactly.  So the people who should decide this issue are not the courts but Congress, correct?
Right, Your Honor. And I -- I think what --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: The states and Congress.

That's right, Your Honor.  And as I -- as I was mentioning in my colloquy with, I believe, Justice Alito  earlier, that's kind of the structure of our system.  States go first.  If Congress doesn't  like it, it overrides.  And, as I think Justice Scalia said for the Court in Arizona Inter Tribal, we respect what Congress said as far as it went but no farther.  And that's kind of the history  of voting and election law in the country to begin with.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: One last question. With respect to history, history is informative  of what's been permitted by Congress because what we're looking for is what understanding  Congress had with respect to elections, correct?
That's right, Your Honor, yeah.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: All right.  And it doesn't talk about the receipt of absentee ballots after elections at all, so we look to the history of whether Congress has accepted it, correct?
I think that does help here, Your Honor.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: All right.  But the attempt by some of the amici here to Bruenize this inquiry and say that history  tells us how elections must be held and on what date and when receipt can happen or not happen,  why is that not an acceptable way to look at this?

Well, I  -- I think the difference between Bruen and here, Your Honor, is that Bruen  --in Bruen, the Court -- the -- the question at issue, you know, whether a restriction on firearms is consistent with our historical tradition of firearm regulation,  there's a rich history addressing precisely that issue, sometimes through analogy, but very  much, I mean, Bruen itself, I believe, I want  to say 40 pages of history just analyzing those things.  We don't have anything like that, a rich history suggesting that Congress was even thinking about locking in Election Day ballot receipt or anything like it.  It was addressing different things.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: All right.  Thank you, counsel.
Thank you, Your Honor.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Justice Kagan?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: I guess, Mr. Stewart, your answers to Justice Sotomayor's questions leave me unsure about what you think about these appeals to history. I mean, you've said that there's not a lot of text here.  I agree with that.  I think that the way this case has been argued all around suggests that that's so.  So  -- so then we're left with history.  Or are we left with history?  You seem to appeal to history sometimes  --Justice Barrett said this -- but then repudiate the appeals to history at other times.  And I guess I want to know what we're supposed to be doing when we're looking at this  statute and deciding this question with respect to all this historical evidence, scant or not scant as it may be.

Sure, Your Honor.  So I  -- I -- I think the best way I can break it down is this, is that history's informative here, and the way it's most informative is that since Congress set  -- I mean, throughout our history and, certainly, since Congress set the federal Election Day, election administration  in our country has been very, very dynamic.  As I tried to highlight in my opener, it was one thing, in-person, on-the-spot qualification checks by fellow voters, ballots were naturally received on Election Day, all those features.  As soon as Congress had a  reason to alter the methods by which a choice was made, it did so.  But the one constant is that the voters, in a popular government, it's most critically the voters, the constant is that the  voters make a final choice of officers by Election Day.  So I think history shows that election administration is dynamic.  States have wide  leeway.  They just have to make sure that the voters make a choice by Election Day.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Thank you.
Thank you, Your Honor.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Justice Gorsuch?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Almost done, Mr. Stewart.  You -- you emphasized to Justice Kagan and many others that the  --the final choice at least has to be done on Election Day and so recall would be a problem for you if  --if it could happen.  But you say that  --that that doesn't happen in Mississippi, that that's -- that's your position, right?
Right.  It's not permitted.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: If recall could happen, that would be a problem for your position?
I think there  -- potentially.  I think there's a  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Because then it wouldn't be a final decision on Election Day, right?
That's right, Your Honor.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Okay.
I think there would still be a factual question, though, of whether  -- I still have not been cited anything to say that recall is actually a thing that can happen in the rule.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: No, I understand. But, if it could happen, that would be a  problem for your theory because the final choice wouldn't have happened on Election Day, right?
Fair, yeah.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Okay.  So you -- you say Mississippi prohibits it.  We -- we've -- we've been through whether that's the case or not.
Very good.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: But let  -- let's say it did.  Let's say there was a law prohibiting recall.  How would it ever be enforced?  Because how is a state to know and how is even a common carrier carrying an envelope to know whether that is a ballot that needs to be recalled?  And who are you going to prosecute?

Well, I think  -- I think it could be enforced similar to -- to other vote  --voter things.  I mean, in our state, there are notarization and affidavit requirements, signing things.  I think one -- if  -- if -- if it were critical to -- for the voter to say that there will be no recall, the voter could say, I hereby commit that I will  not attempt to or recall this package in any way, shape, or form.  They could just add that, sign it.  I take the point about proof problems, but, I mean, gosh, Justice Gorsuch, I mean, violating state election laws in a state that  really is antifraud and really takes wide measures to enforce its laws, that would be quite a thing for a voter to do.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, in my hypothetical, which, you know, you say is unlikely to swing an election and all of that on recall, but as soon -- you know, if --if history teaches anything, scant or not scant,  it's that as soon as something's allowed, it will happen eventually, right?  And, you know, so -- so somebody --my hypothetical happens and everybody recalls their ballots.  I'm just not sure what recourse  the state would have against people who violated its anti-recall law.
I mean, if people are, say, recalling things through a common carrier,  there's going to be some record that they recalled those things.  A state could  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: How's a state ever going to find out about it?
I mean, I think the same  --the same way it would find --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: It's going to go -- you're going to go prosecute individuals?

I mean, Your Honor, I'd say, like, if somebody is lying in an affidavit that they're not going to recall something, I mean, if  --if people are doing that with impunity, we have quite a problem, but it is a problem that the state can address and enforce  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: I just don't know how they'd ever find out about it.

I mean, I think you -- obviously, you know, some crimes are harder to  find out and prosecute than others, Your Honor, but I think it's still -- I mean, people can do things, try to, like, tamper with ballots, all that sort of thing.  I think it's just still a  matter of respecting the statute.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Thank you.
Thank you, Justice Gorsuch.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Justice Kavanaugh?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: When did Mississippi switch to this method?
2020.  In 2024, it added common carriers.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: And why?
It was first because of the pandemic.  I have -- I don't know that  there's necessarily an answer about why as to the 2024 one in a clear -- in a clear way.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: And the other side makes a point when we're looking at history, to the extent historical practice is relevant,  that it only became widespread to allow it to be mailed by Election Day in more recent years and that the predominant approach was to require receipt by Election Day throughout the historical practice you cite, until very recently.  How are we supposed to think about that?

I mean, I think it's the same way to think about, I -- I think, the broader history of election law, is, when  -- when states have kind of seen a problem, they've adapted and adjusted in  --often in -- in the direction of allow -- making sure more votes can be counted.  I mean, that was obviously a big thing when absentee voting started to become a prominent thing.  You know,  certainly, we cared for much about our history of people showing up in person, but we realized that was very difficult for people away from home and that we wanted to, you know, kind of widen the tent and make it -- make it so that people could vote.  And I think perhaps another realization, even though we've had UOCAVA for  40 years, Justice Kavanaugh, is that for military voters in particular, this is a perennial challenge about making sure that they  can actually get their ballots in on time.  I mean, that's perhaps why UOCAVA voters in particular are a very popular group for post-Election Day ballot receipt.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Would you say that the states that require receipt by Election Day are disenfranchising voters?
No, you're not  -- they're not, Your Honor.  I mean, a reasonable ballot deadline does not do that.  I would  asterisk just there are the practical barriers for those overseas military voters.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: But, for the citizens who are not within that class, you would not use the term "disenfranchisement" to say it has to be received by Election Day, November 3rd, rather than -- I guess it would be five business days -- November 10th?  You would not use that term to describe that, correct?
I would not.  Correct, Your Honor.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: And then picking up on Justice Alito's questions, Professor Pildes and others have said that late-arriving ballots open up a risk of what might destabilize the election results.  "If the  apparent winner the morning after the election ends up losing due to late -arriving ballots, charges of a rigged election could explode. The longer after Election Day any significant changes in vote totals take place, the greater  the risk that the losing side will cry that the election has been stolen."  And my question is  -- my questions, one, is that a real concern?  Two, does that factor into how we think about how to resolve the scant text and the maybe conflicting or evolving history here?

I think  -- I certainly respect the perception.  I think one thing notable in this case and I think helpful is that there -- there -- there has not been much  --much of a showing about actual fraud from post-Election Day ballot receipt itself. I mean, that was --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, I think Justice Alito referred to and I think this quote refers to the appearance of fraud.  And is that a real concern?  Is that something we  should be thinking about, confidence in the election process?  Just  --just curious how we factor that in here.

Right, and I think it would go back to the same answer I had for  Justice Alito about scant -- you know, there -- simple text, straightforward text, and respecting the limits of that text, and looking  at the animated history, I think it really was  -- it was the double-voting fraud concern. I don't know that people have that particular concern.  I think, you know, obviously, people can be, you know, unhappy when a -- a result flips.  I think Congress may be able to take measures to address that.  But I think there's  no good evidence that Congress was doing that beyond preventing double-voting in this context.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: But, if you have to have a deadline, which you acknowledged, and if having a deadline of November 3rd rather  than November 10th doesn't -- for receipt, doesn't disenfranchise anyone, why wouldn't it make more sense to  -- to take account in some respect of that concern as we think about how  the text and history fit together?

Well, I think, I mean, something that Congress was clearly, I think,  trying to do was adopting a simple rule in this text.  And I think a very simple rule is everybody must cast their ballot by Election Day.  I mean, that's quite administrable.  I  mean, if you have an Election Day ballot receipt deadline, there are certainly things to commend that.  I think you're alluding to some  of those, Justice Kavanaugh.  But there's also a question of, when do I vote?  You know, I'm not sure.  You know, do I need to do it 7, you know, whatever it is? Whereas, you know, if somebody wants to get all the information possible, they like voting on  Election Day, you have a pretty nice, clear, simple rule, and that seems to dovetail quite well with the  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, the simple rule, but, if it arrives on November 11th, you're out.

Right, but I think that's kind of baked into the risks you always get when you're doing -- there are always some  risks, you know, regrettably with mail-in voting.  You can eliminate some of those risks by voting in person, but --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: The risks would seem the same no matter whether it's November 3rd or November 10th, in other words, that it could take longer than a week for the mail to get there.

The risk is there, but I  -- I think, if you have Election Day ballot receipt  --and I -- I think what we're addressing, I think, are more -- the way I might frame the issues are these are policy points.  The question is, did Congress wall off  states from debating these policy points?  I think the answer is no.  And I think states could very reasonably say, you know, look, we  -- we do want to get counting and get a result very fast, but we are concerned about these military  voters, we do want voters to be able to get whatever  --whatever information they want.  I mean, the weekend before, you know, that used to be a big deal in elections at least.  Maybe  it still could be in the future.  And I think a state could say:  Hey, look, federal law didn't wall us off from doing this.  We get that it has some things about it that other states might weigh differently, but we want to allow that for our voters.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, I take your point, but it really goes to just thinking about what Election Day or day of election means.  But I -- I take your point.  Thank you.
Thank you, Your Honor.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Justice Barrett?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: So I want to be clear about what your definition of finality  requires.  Would it require finality if the vote arrives by Election Day as well?  So let's  -- let's imagine an absentee ballot that's put in the mail or sent by common carrier well in advance of Election Day and does  --is received and put in the ballot box by Election Day.  Does that one have to be final?  Or, in other words, would it be a problem for you that the U.S. Postal -- Postal Service permits recall for those ballots that are sent in advance?  I guess what I'm asking is, do you have the same problem either way?  You've -- you've taken a lot of questions, and I have those questions, about what the effect of this recall ability is.  And I guess my question is, I want to understand what your definition of finality is and whether it applies to the earlier absentee ballots as well.  Do they have to be final such that it would be illegal to recall them pursuant to whatever regulation the post office has?
Right.  I think I got it, Justice Barrett.  Let me see if I can do my  -- my best on it. I mean, I think, in theory, if Election Day has not passed, there could be a window for somebody to --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: So it would be okay? It wouldn't be illegal for somebody to recall a ballot before Election Day?  I guess I don't  understand why --
Well, I mean, if a state allowed that, Your Honor.  I mean, we don't -- we don't allow it.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: So it would be okay for the state  --I know you don't allow it.
Right.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: But I guess what I'm under -- I guess I'm struggling because, if  your definition of the election or the vote or casting the vote requires finality, I'm trying to understand why that would be different before the election  -- when I'm saying before the election, I'm talking about receipt -- for earlier-sent absentee ballots and for later-sent.  It seems like the same rule should apply regardless.  But it seems like you're not  -- you're saying something different.
Yeah, I  -- I -- I'm having a  -- I guess I'm having a hard time conceiving kind of a dual-track rule in -- in  -- in that circumstance.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: So would it be  -- let me try to put it this way.  Would it be illegal for a state to permit absentee voting but permit recall or  --or just kind of be silent about this Postal Service regulation that permits recall or anything a common carrier did to permit recall?  Is recall a  problem even if it's a possibility for those earlier absentee ballots?  Because you can't consider them final. All these questions that you've been taking are about whether you could really consider the ballot to be final if you could recall it.  So  I'm asking whether that same finality test applies for the earlier ballots.
And I'm not sure, Your Honor.  I mean, I think  -- I --I guess I just keep coming back to you can't recall or change your vote or  -- or make any effort like that --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: And that's true no matter when you send it.
I think, I mean, certainly, in our state, and I think -- I think that's right, Your Honor.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: But I mean as a matter of the federal law.  It just seems to me that your definition has to be consistent, and it sounds like you're changing it for the  earlier absentee ballots and saying finality has some kind of different force for the later-received absentee ballots.

Right.  Well, I -- I think a state has to do whatever it would need to do to guarantee that on Election Day, all ballots  --you know, every -- every cast vote is final and cannot be recalled.  I -- I -- I'm having --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: But it doesn't have to be final at the time it's sent because it's okay to recall it.  If you send it two weeks in advance and you change your mind, that's not a problem.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Okay.  I'll withdraw.
Yeah, I guess I'm having trouble seeing how  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Okay.
-- the federal Election Day statute itself would necessarily allow that, Your Honor.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Well, it's about your definition of election.  It's about your  definition of what it means to cast a vote, but let's put that aside.  Obviously, there's a lot of talk about history in this case.  Well, the Electoral  Count Reform Act was passed in 2022, and for the first time, it defined Election Day. Should that matter?  So should we be looking at how Congress understood Election Day to mean in the period of voting, what it thought in 2022, or should we be looking at the late 19th century and the Civil War practices?

I think most vitally it still remains 1845 is the key date, especially given that we have statutes that are trying to manifestly achieve uniformity and what is required of all federal offices.  So I  --I do think 1845 is the key date.  And I  --

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: So Congress carried over in 2022 the same understanding of Election Day that had persisted throughout?
I think that's right, final choice of an officer.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Okay.  Thank you.
Thank you, Your Honor.

roles.role_title: Chief Justice of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Justice Jackson?

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: So let me just clarify.  This case is not about a Mississippi  practice or policy related to recalling ballots, is that right?
That's right, Your Honor.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: So I  --I guess I'm a little confused about those kinds of policy questions, and I guess -- I think that the Constitution's allocation of responsibility  here actually makes this case about who decides.  I mean, there are a lot of policy questions.  Justice Alito ran through several of them, who gets to receive the ballot, how long after can they be submitted, does it have to be postmarked.  I suppose we can add is recall allowed, et cetera, et cetera.  But the question, I think, is whether Congress has precluded the states from making those calls, drawing those lines, and your position as I understand it is no.
That's correct, Your Honor.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: That the  -- that the scantness of Election Day in the federal  statutes actually is a point in your favor because it indicates that Congress was leaving  it to the states to draw the various lines that might arise in this circumstance.  Is that right?

That's right, Your Honor.  And that's reinforced, for example, by  -- by the 1866 statute, which shows that when Congress wanted to be really prescriptive in this area, it was very prescriptive.  It  described this is what the states have to do and so forth.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: So, if we were focused, really focused on what we're asked to answer here, which is, is the -- are the states preempted by federal law from having post-Election Day ballot deadlines, you would say no?
No.  No.  Congress just didn't decide that.

roles.role_title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States
roles.institution_name: Supreme Court of the United States

text_blocks.text: Let me ask you about the history with respect to Bruen.  I -- I -- I guess I'm not sure I understood your answer to Justice Sotomayor because it seems to me that Bruen is not even the right methodology by which to be thinking about this.  Bruen applied to the Second Amendment because the Second Amendment incorporated a preexisting right.  And the point of the history and tradition test was to try to evaluate the contours of that right.  We -- we don't have that dynamic here.
